newsitem.title: USA: Chemical heir loses control of Du Pont estate.
newsitem.headline: Chemical heir loses control of Du Pont estate.

text.p: The wealth of chemicals heir John du Pont, a convicted murderer awaiting sentencing, will be managed by three trustees including his sister, according to an agreement ending a family legal dispute, the Philadelphia Inquirer reported on Tuesday.
The agreement, settling a suit begun last year, was filed in Delaware County Orphans Court on Monday and will be reviewed by Judge Leo Sereni on Friday, the newspaper said.

Du Pont, 58, was in Norristown State Hospital after a jury on Feb. 25 found him guilty but mentally ill in the 1996 murder of wrestler David Schultz. Sentencing was set for April 22 and du Pont faced a 40-year maximum term.
Du Pont, a onetime coach and wrestling patron at Villanova University, built an Olympic-scale training centre on his 800-acre Foxcatcher Farm estate and hired Schultz as coach.

The guardianship petition sought to have the Orphans Court name du Pont's sister, Jean Shehan, 73, of Coral Gables, Fla., and his nephew, James McConnell Jr., 43, of Rapidan, Va., as guardians, the Inquirer said.
The petition noted du Pont inherited $88 million a decade ago. Estimates of the estate's current value ranged from $120 million to more than $200 million.

According to the newspaper, the agreement allowed du Pont to select the trustees and gave them control of his assets and over medical and financial decisions affecting him. It required them to consult du Pont but not to bow to his views.

The trustees also include Terry McDonnell, a friend and long-time employee, and Bryn Mawr Trust, du Pont's bank. In the document, du Pont acknowledged his need for guidance in light of his near-term prospects but held out hope he could return to his home, the Inquirer reported.
Meanwhile, du Pont faced yet another legal problem. A federal lawsuit filed last month accused him of discriminating against four black wrestlers who were part of the team he was training.

They contended du Pont paid them smaller stipends than white athletes and did not invite them to live on his estate. He finally dismissed three of them, saying he wanted to eliminate the colour black from his life, they said.
The suit said du Pont's obsession associated the colour with death. It accused him of violating federal civil rights and fair housing laws.
